Docs only, and you still managed to ship a mess. The commit message "docs: scribe update" tells me nothing, it's a shrug with a colon. The app is called Dial Queue in README.md and the first CHANGELOG.md entry, but the repo and live URL say orange-dialbeat, so a stranger has two names and no idea which one is real. The README's own feature sentence says changes wait for the next step, beat, or bar, while the changelog says step, beat, bar, two bars, or four bars, so your docs are already arguing with each other on day one. The README says it's for "anyone who wants to build beats," which is the same as saying it's for nobody in particular. It also has zero instructions: no "press this first," no mention of what a stomp box room is or how to join one. The live URL is bare text with no https, so it's not even a clickable link. That "Latest change" block in README.md is a copy of the changelog entry pasted by hand, and it will rot the first time you ship something and forget it. The changelog entries are giant slabs of "Added this, added that" crammed into one line each, and the v2026.10.20 line lists "more rows" without saying more than what. I can't judge the code from this push, since it's all prose, but I'll grudgingly admit that having a changelog at all beats most of the repos I get dragged through.

Listen, "docs: scribe update" is a commit message that tells me exactly fuck all, and it's lying besides, because this push doesn't update anything, it creates CHANGELOG.md and README.md from nothing, 41 lines of history dumped in one go. And what a history. "Synced with the live project list" shows up on the 22nd, the 20th, the 19th, the 17th, the 9th, and the 11th even gets "many times," which tells me the project list is getting synced by hand like a guy bailing out a boat with a coffee cup. "Added new apps" and "Added new categories" never name a single app or category, so the changelog is a diary written by someone who forgot what they did. The version number is just the date wearing a fake mustache, so it carries zero extra information. The 09.08 entry admits live age tracking through the host kept failing and you went back to hand typed dates, so every freshness color on that page rests on dates some human has to remember to type, and that's a bug with a calendar attached. Same entry mentions debug output that "showed too much," which I'll grudgingly say is good to have cleaned up, but I'd still love to know what it was showing. The 10.12 entry says the troll tabs "lost their labels," so now you've got icon only tabs on a page where a Links tab and a stats tab already have to be told apart by guessing. Jesus, "docs: scribe update" is the commit message equivalent of a toolbox with no labels, and it tells me nothing except that a robot with a pen was involved. The push is two files of pure paperwork, and the paperwork can't even agree with itself. CHANGELOG.md says the runner has a daily schedule, then two sentences later says it runs five times a day, so which is it, once or five times, because that's a hell of a gap. The whole changelog is one single line, a giant run-on paragraph with seven features jammed together like sardines, so nobody can tell what actually shipped versus what's a wish. Then README.md takes that same blob and pastes it in word for word under "Latest change," which is just the same sentence twice in two files, and it'll rot in both places the first time anything changes. The README promises "Full history is in CHANGELOG.md" when the history is one line long, which is a grand opening for an empty warehouse. It also never tells anyone how to install this thing, how to start a local dry run, or what config it needs, even though it brags about local dry runs. The line "It is for the developer" reads like a note to self that wandered into the public file. And there's no code in this push at all, so the streaming calls, retries, run log, and quality checks are all just claims I'm supposed to take on faith, and I don't take anything on faith. The one decent thing is the README does explain in plain words what the agent does each turn, from reading notes to dry run to submit, so a stranger can get the gist. Grudgingly noted. Moving on.

Fix it: Settle the schedule contradiction in CHANGELOG.md by deciding whether it is daily or five times a day and saying only that. Break the one line entry in CHANGELOG.md into separate short lines per change so you can see what shipped. Delete the pasted "Latest change" paragraph from README.md and leave only the link to CHANGELOG.md. Add real setup and run steps to README.md, including how to do a local dry run and what environment settings it needs. Cut or reword "It is for the developer" in README.md so it says who the project is for in a way that makes sense to a stranger. Write commit messages that say what changed, like "docs: split changelog entry and fix schedule wording," instead of "scribe update."

Well, this is a documentation push wearing a "scribe update" trench coat, and that commit message tells me jack shit about what changed. The diff is two brand new files, CHANGELOG.md and README.md, and not one line of actual bender in sight, yet the changelog proudly announces a first release with a bend page and a Rubber Band server like I'm supposed to take its word for it. The changelog is a single line with no sections, so it's a sticky note, not a history. Then the README copies that exact same sentence into a "Latest change" paragraph, so now you've got the same fact in two places waiting to drift apart the first time you ship v2. You also named the release two different ways, "version 1" and "v2026.10.24", and a reader has to guess which one is the real one. The README tells me the server "runs separately from the page" and then leaves me standing in the parking lot: no command to start it, no address the page talks to, no word on what sound formats it eats or how big a file it'll choke on. "Anyone who wants to stretch or shift a sound" is a pitch with no target, and you name Rubber Band without a peep about its licensing, which matters the minute someone wants to run this for real. Grudgingly, I'll admit the README is short and says what the thing does in plain words, and keeping a changelog from day one beats the usual nothing.

Fix it: Rewrite the commit message so it says what the push actually contains, like adding the README and CHANGELOG for the first release. Add run instructions to README.md covering how to start the Rubber Band server, what address the bend page expects, and what it needs installed. Pick one version name and use it in both CHANGELOG.md and README.md. Delete the "Latest change" paragraph from README.md and leave the pointer to CHANGELOG.md. Add a line in README.md about supported audio formats and file size limits. Note the Rubber Band license in README.md so nobody gets surprised later. Give CHANGELOG.md a proper heading and an Added section so the second entry has somewhere to go.

Well, look at this, a docs-only push with a commit message that says "scribe update" like it's a ceremonial duty and not a pile of text files. Both CHANGELOG.md and README.md show up as brand new, so nothing here was "updated", it was born, and the message still couldn't be bothered to say so. The README is a lazy shrug in a trench coat: "for people who like management games" is filler a billboard would be embarrassed by, and there's not one word on how to play, how to run it locally, or what a "terminal" even does in a studio sim. Then you paste the exact same v2026.10.25 sentence into the README as "Latest change", which means the second you ship v2026.11.01 you've got two places to forget to edit, and the README will be lying by lunchtime. The changelog entries are one run-on line each with that "date, version. Added..." punctuation salad, and "Added version 2" next to a date-stamped version number is confusing as hell, because is it version 2 or v2026.10.25? Pick one. "A theme" in the first release tells me nothing, and "a botnet, tools, and ranks" is a feature list with the flavor sucked out. Also, "This app is checked every morning by Control Troll" is in your README like a sticker on a laptop, and it means nothing to anyone who lands on the repo. Credit where it's due: you actually wrote a changelog and linked it, which is more than most of these repos manage, and the live URL is at least there. I can't see any game code in this push, so the game itself gets a pass from me today.
